text: CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Tirtawening Bandung ChatWater Stages 1–4: a practical worked example Water supply, wastewater collection and Bojongsoang wastewater treatment Prepared October 30, 2026 | Reference water year: 2023 | English input guide We use a real Indonesian utility that operates both water and wastewater services. We combine published utility information with clearly identified historical proxies and example assumptions to show how to complete the whole ChatWater workflow. [1–6] This is a report-ready demonstration, not a verified Tirtawening emissions inventory, an approved investment, or evidence of utility endorsement. How to use this guide Step What we enter or prepare 1 Assess Utility profile; ECAM water and wastewater inputs; an additional climate-risk and water-safety worksheet. 2 Identify actions A short list of justified actions, including custom wastewater and resilience actions.

3 Project plan Eight planning fields, a 104-week schedule, an illustrative budget and measurable indicators. 4 Financing Proposal All preliminary-concept fields, financing choices, an eight-section narrative and preparation gaps. Our evidence labels Label Meaning R | Reported A figure or operating fact from an identified public source. We retain its year and boundary. D | Derived Our arithmetic using reported data. This does not make the result a utility-certified measurement. P | Proxy A historical value or a different statistical definition used temporarily for the demonstration. A | Assumed An illustrative number, target, cost, risk score or planning choice. It is not a reported utility fact. Unknown The verified input is unavailable. For actual reporting, we keep it unknown rather than treating it as zero. Enter numbers without thousands separators. Use annual totals unless stated otherwise.

For Unknown, use the ? control or leave the field blank; do not type the word into a numeric box. Bracketed source numbers refer to the linked references. We inspected the live forms. CREAT and WHO climate-resilient Water Safety Plan modules are labeled “Not active yet.” We therefore supply their additional inputs as manual planning notes, not as completed in-app assessments. We do not claim that this Bandung case was run and validated end to end. [16] Evidence-based worked example | 1

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG The real utility and the limits of our evidence Perumda Tirtawening Kota Bandung operates drinking-water and domestic wastewater services. Bojongsoang is in Kabupaten Bandung and serves wastewater from Kota Bandung. We keep the service area and the plant location distinct. Its treatment train uses anaerobic, facultative and maturation ponds, with inlet pumping, screening and grit removal. It is not an activated-sludge plant. [3, 4] Published indicator Value and reporting basis Water customers; active domestic connections 169,373 total customers; 165,680 active domestic connections, 2023 [1]. These are different categories. Population served; service-area population 965,283 served; 2,793,549 in the reported service area, 2023 [1]. Administrative population 2,569,107, 2023 [1]. Do not interchange this with the larger service-area denominator. Water service coverage; supply hours 34.55%; 18 hours/day, 2023 [1].

Coverage uses the source’s service-area denominator. Non-revenue water (NRW) 39.42%, 2023 [1]. NRW includes unbilled authorized use as well as losses. Production capacity; reservoir storage 2,789 L/s installed; 667 L/s unavailable; 28,400 m³ reservoir capacity, 2023 [1]. Pipe length 126,300 m transmission; 1,487,522 m distribution, 2023 [1]. Water volume reported by BPS 36,622,383 m³ “air disalurkan,” 2023 [2]. It is not explicitly identified as ECAM billed consumption. Tariff and cost recovery Average tariff IDR 6,638/m³; full-cost-recovery indicator 85.53%, 2023 [1]. Company financial context Revenue IDR 331.032 billion; operating expense IDR 314.617 billion; net profit IDR 6.432 billion, 2023 [1]. Existing plans and staffing RPAM exists; business plan 2022–2026; RISPAM 2021–2040; 700 employees in 2023 [1]. The 2024 performance book reports 2023 operations. We use this consistent, traceable water reference year, not a claim about the latest utility performance.

The book reports an energy-cost indicator of IDR 79/m³, not electricity consumption in kWh. It cannot substitute for meter readings. [1] Our weakest evidence is annual wastewater and energy data: Bojongsoang’s available detailed monthly dataset is from 2019. We do not relabel it as measured 2023 data. All investment amounts and future benefits below are assumptions. Evidence-based worked example | 2

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Utility profile and general settings We open ChatWater in English, use a separate DEMO utility profile and create a new assessment. The utility profile can be shared by several assessments, so we check its association before editing an existing profile. [16] Profile field Our entry Utility name DEMO | Perumda Tirtawening Kota Bandung City / regency, province Kota Bandung, West Java, Indonesia; Bojongsoang WWTP is in Kabupaten Bandung. Water supply; sewer network; central IPAL We operate it, for all three [R: 3]. Household septic tanks and pits Not our responsibility [A: individual household containment is outside this modeled operating boundary]. Desludging and faecal sludge treatment Not sure / not answered. Capital budget for new investment Partly; co-financing needed [A].

This is not an assessment of current borrowing capacity. In-house engineering capacity Some [A]. We assume internal operations staff plus specialist support. Operational data Partly measured, partly estimated [A: describes this example dataset]. General field Our entry Service type Water and wastewater Assessment name DEMO Tirtawening Bandung | 2023 reference + historical proxies Period From 2023-01-01 to 2024-01-01. The end date is exclusive: 365 days. Country; currency Indonesia; IDR Global warming potential IPCC Fifth Assessment Report, without climate–carbon feedbacks: CH₄ = 28; N₂O = 265. Paste into Comments We use verified 2023 water indicators, historical 2019 Bojongsoang proxies and explicit test assumptions. Energy, nitrogen, sludge, discharge balance and emission-factor applicability are unverified.

This is a worked example, not a measured inventory or an approved project. We exclude onsite sanitation, fuels, trucking and downstream sludge management. Zero bypass means an assumed test boundary, not observed zero pollution. Climate evidence from 2025–2026 informs forward planning only. See this guide’s labeled input tables and sources. CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Water supply inputs We add one substage each for Water abstraction, Water treatment and Water distribution. These aggregate the utility system for the example. We do not copy total utility electricity into each substage.

Field in ChatWater Enter this value Unit Basis Water supply: resident population 2793549 people R [1] Water abstraction: volume abstracted / conveyed 64000000 m³/year A Water abstraction: grid energy consumed 1000000 kWh/year A Water treatment: volume treated 62000000 m³/year A Water treatment: grid energy consumed 800000 kWh/year A Water distribution: serviced population 965283 people R [1] Water distribution: volume distributed 60452927 m³/year D + P Water distribution: grid energy consumed 1200000 kWh/year A Water distribution: authorized consumption 37226912 m³/year D + A Water distribution: billed consumption 36622383 m³/year P [2] Grid factor in each water substage 0.677 kgCO₂e/kWh A Why these volumes are internally consistent For the test only, we map the BPS volume to billed consumption. We then calculate distribution input = 36,622,383 ÷ (1 − 0.3942) = 60,452,927 m³, rounded. We assume unbilled authorized use is 1% of distribution input, or 604,529 m³.

Authorized consumption becomes 36,622,383 + 604,529 = 37,226,912 m³. This reproduces 39.42% NRW by construction. Water loss is 38.42% because it excludes unbilled authorized use. Neither the distribution volume nor the match to NRW independently validates the BPS-to-billing mapping. Confirm system input and customer billing records before actual reporting. Optional fields and switches Choose Yes for water-efficiency inputs in distribution to expose authorized and billed consumption. If a treatment description is requested, enter “Aggregated conventional surface-water treatment plus other sources; verify plant-specific allocation.” Official sources include river water, springs and boreholes; do not describe all water as pumped groundwater. [3] Keep pumping-efficiency and electromechanical-efficiency modules off until pump head, flow and electrical measurements are available. Keep stage operating costs unknown.

For an optional training-only total water energy cost, enter IDR 4,500,000,000 = 3,000,000 kWh × assumed IDR 1,500/kWh. Do not treat company operating expense as the cost of one process. Evidence-based worked example | 4

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | What the wastewater evidence supports We add Wastewater collection and Wastewater treatment. We represent the connected sewer and Bojongsoang pond train, not every household in Bandung. We leave Onsite sanitation outside this run. Wastewater pumping stations include Gumuruh and Cijaura; Bojongsoang also has inlet screw pumps. The energy allocation must avoid counting any pump twice. [3, 4] Item What we use and what it means Treatment technology [R] Screening and grit removal, then anaerobic, facultative and maturation ponds in parallel sets A and B [4]. Historical design flow [R] 80,835 m³/day [5]. This is a design reference, not current demonstrated treatment capacity. Historical inlet flow [D] 24,566,522 m³ in 2019, derived by multiplying each monthly average daily flow by calendar days and summing [5]. Historical outlet flow [D] 18,829,038 m³ in 2019, calculated in the same way [5].

Historical flow discrepancy [D] 5,737,484 m³ between inlet and outlet. The available records do not close this balance. Historical influent BOD load [D] 2,250,840.14 kg/year, calculated from monthly inlet flows and monthly BOD results [5]. Historical effluent BOD load [D] 438,036.28 kg/year, calculated from monthly outlet flows and monthly BOD results [5]. What is missing A verified 2023 sewer population, bypass record, energy allocation, nitrogen balance, sludge removals and representative pond emission factor. Two corrections that matter The 2019 flow table prints annual-average figures that do not agree with its monthly rows. We use the monthly rows and show the calculation in Appendix A. We do not copy the inconsistent printed average. [5] Monthly BOD observations are not a continuous, flow-proportional sampling program. January and February results cover set A; later results cover A and B.

Our annual load is a historical approximation, not a certified annual pollutant mass balance. [5] Our explicit demonstration choice We use the derived 2019 inlet volume and influent BOD as proxies. To create a simple closed-flow test, we assume the same annual volume is collected, treated and discharged, with no reuse or bypass in the modeled branch. This deliberately replaces the unexplained historical outlet balance. It does not establish that Bojongsoang actually has no bypass, water losses, withdrawals or reuse. Evidence-based worked example | 5

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Wastewater collection inputs Field in ChatWater Enter this value Unit Basis Sanitation: resident population 2569107 people R, 2023 [1] Sanitation: wastewater generated Unknown m³/year No city total Population connected to sewer network 500000 people A Volume of collected wastewater 24566522 m³/year D + P, 2019 Collected wastewater discharged untreated 0 m³/year A: test only Collected wastewater sent to treatment 24566522 m³/year D + P + A BOD₅ load in collected wastewater 2250840.14 kg/year D + P, 2019 Total nitrogen in collected wastewater 491330.44 kg N/year A: 20 mg/L Grid electricity for collection 500000 kWh/year A Grid emission factor 0.677 kgCO₂e/kWh A CH₄ factor for sewer collection 0 kgCH₄/kgBOD A: flowing N₂O factor for sewer collection 0 kgN₂O-N/kgN A CH₄ factor for untreated discharge 0.021 kgCH₄/kgBOD A, method N₂O factor for untreated discharge 0.005 kgN₂O-N/kgN A, method We select flowing-sewer assumptions for the demonstration.

Zero collection factors do not prove the real sewer is always aerobic or free of sediment, stagnation and emissions. Untreated-discharge factors have no numerical effect while the assumed untreated volume is zero. [7] The 500,000-person value is an example denominator, not a verified 2023 customer count. It must not be used to claim current sewer coverage. The citywide sanitation-access percentage includes onsite services and is not Bojongsoang’s sewer coverage. [6] Extra settings Keep pump-efficiency calculations off until measurements are available. Assign collection electricity to upstream sewer pumping and assign inlet screw pumps to treatment. Mark actual stage costs unknown. If a total wastewater energy-cost example is needed, use IDR 1,875,000,000 = 1,250,000 kWh × assumed IDR 1,500/kWh. We do not estimate citywide wastewater generation by equating it to the sewer inlet flow. Infiltration, stormwater connections and non-sewered households make those quantities different.
For an actual inventory, untreated discharge and sewer factors remain unknown until the operating records support them. Evidence-based worked example | 6

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Bojongsoang treatment inputs Field in ChatWater Enter this value Unit Basis Serviced population 500000 people A Volume of treated wastewater 24566522 m³/year D + P Discharged effluent to water body 24566522 m³/year A: closed flow Influent BOD₅ load 2250840.14 kg/year D + P Effluent BOD₅ load 614163.05 kg/year A: 25 mg/L Influent total nitrogen load 491330.44 kg N/year A: 20 mg/L Effluent total nitrogen load 294798.26 kg N/year A: 12 mg/L Grid electricity consumed 750000 kWh/year A Grid emission factor 0.677 kgCO₂e/kWh A Sludge removed, dry weight 150000 kg dry/year A BOD₅ removed as sludge 150000 kg BOD/year A: separate CH₄ emission factor: treatment 0.48 kgCH₄/kgBOD P: deep pond N₂O emission factor: treatment 0 kgN₂O-N/kgN P: anaerobic CH₄ emission factor: discharge 0.021 kgCH₄/kgBOD A: river type N₂O emission factor: discharge 0.005 kgN₂O-N/kgN A: Tier 1 The pollutant-load equation is volume (m³) × concentration (mg/L) ÷ 1,000.

Concentration and mass are different inputs. For example, 24,566,522 × 25 ÷ 1,000 = 614,163.05 kg BOD/year. Do not type “25” into the annual BOD- load field. We enter sludge dry mass and sludge BOD separately. Their equal values are coincidental assumptions for this test, not a universal conversion. Pond sludge can remain stored for years; this removal quantity is not a measured annual sludge production rate. For the test, select No for fuel engines, captured biogas, trucked reused water, avoided reuse emissions and sludge-management calculations. These switches mean “outside this run,” not verified absence at the utility. An anaerobic pond can emit methane even when no biogas is collected. Do not select “covered lagoon” merely to make treatment emissions zero. Evidence-based worked example | 7

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Factor choices and numerical checks The pond train needs a better factor before actual reporting For a reproducible screening run, we choose “Anaerobic deep lagoon (>2m depth)” for treatment CH₄. The historical study gives 3.5 m for anaerobic ponds, with shallower downstream ponds. Applying 0.48 to the entire aggregated train is a proxy, not a validated site factor. ECAM specifically advises additional or customized factors for treatment trains with multiple technologies. [5, 7] We duplicate the assessment and test 0.12, the shallow/facultative pond default, to show sensitivity. Neither endpoint is a confidence bound or a complete model of the serial train. We do not average factors by pond area or multiply both factors by the full influent load. A verified mass balance and suitable multi-stage method are required. The treatment N₂O default of zero is an anaerobic-pond screening assumption.

It does not demonstrate zero N₂O across facultative and maturation ponds. Likewise, 0.005 for discharge is a generic Tier 1 factor; assess the receiving water before substituting a site-specific or nutrient-impacted factor. [7] Check Expected demonstration result Water balance Billed ≤ authorized ≤ distributed ≤ treated ≤ abstracted. NRW; water loss 39.42% NRW; 38.42% water loss. Rounded-volume differences are negligible. Water electricity 3,000,000 kWh; 2,031 tCO₂e at factor 0.677. Wastewater electricity 1,250,000 kWh; 846.25 tCO₂e at factor 0.677. All included electricity 4,250,000 kWh; 2,877.25 tCO₂e. This is an assumed scenario, not reported utility emissions. WWTP energy intensity 0.0305 kWh/m³ treated. This low assumed value is for ponds and pumping, not activated-sludge aeration. BOD load removal 1,636,677.09 kg/year, or approximately 72.71% of influent load, under the test assumptions. ECAM treatment CH₄ uses (influent BOD − BOD removed as sludge) × treatment factor × CH₄ GWP.

It does not additionally subtract effluent BOD in that equation. Discharged-water emissions use effluent loads separately. Follow the implemented methodology rather than replacing its formula with a different mass-balance equation. [7, equations 80 and 99] We confirm values only after checking their intended use. An app “confirmed” flag is not scientific verification. Unknown values can leave totals incomplete. We do not use an aggregate emissions total from this exercise as Tirtawening’s inventory or claim any modeled reduction as achieved. Evidence-based worked example | 8

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Additional climate-risk inputs CREAT is not active in this version. We retain this worksheet with our assessment and paste its key findings into Stage 3 and Stage 4. We use an asset–hazard–consequence–action structure inspired by CREAT, without claiming to have run the EPA tool. [8, 16] Input Our example entry Planning horizon 2027–2040 [A]. The investment lasts 104 weeks after funding, with longer-lived assets tested beyond completion. Assets and service dependencies Cikalong raw-water intake; source-to-treatment supply; selected distribution zones; Gumuruh/Cijaura pumping; Bojongsoang inlet, power equipment and ponds [3, 4]. Exact elevations and boundaries remain to be surveyed. Observed dry-season evidence Tirtawening’s September 2, 2026 notice reports lower Cikalong raw-water flow and distribution disruption [9]. It does not quantify a climate-change trend.

Observed flood evidence Local government reported flooding and a levee breach in Desa Bojongsoang in February 2025 [10]. This establishes local hazard context, not proven inundation of the plant. Projection information to obtain BMKG rainfall projections and local observations for source catchments and assets. BMKG’s portal uses CMIP6 scenarios and 25 km data; local hydraulic design needs finer analysis [11]. Scenario choice Review SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, near-term 2021–2050 relative to 1981–2010, plus observed extremes [A selection using the BMKG framework]. No local percentage change has been extracted here. Dry-season stress test Assume available source yield is 20% lower for 30 days [A, not a forecast]. Calculate storage, demand restrictions and priority-service needs from actual operating data. Wet-weather stress test Assume peak sewer inflow reaches 1.5 times measured dry-weather peak, and a 6-hour power outage occurs [A]. Use measured peak flow, not annual average, for design.

Flood design input Unknown. Survey ground, equipment and water levels; obtain flood depths, duration and return-period estimates. Do not use a news-reported road depth as plant design level. We separate three statements: an observed service disruption, a plausible climate-related vulnerability, and a quantified future projection. Only the first two are supported here. Climate attribution and local future hazard magnitudes remain preparation tasks. Evidence-based worked example | 9

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 1 | Water safety and risk priorities Tirtawening already reported an RPAM. We propose updating it with climate considerations, not creating a plan on the assumption none exists. WHO guidance supports source-to-consumer risk management and climate resilience. [1, 12] Hazard and consequence Initial priority [A] Controls and evidence needed Dry-season low source flow reduces supply continuity. Likelihood 4 × consequence 4 = 16, high Update drought triggers, source monitoring and demand management; verify available storage and alternative supply quality. Heavy rain changes raw-water quality and may overwhelm treatment control. 3 × 4 = 12, high Track turbidity, treatment performance and disinfectant residual; establish operating limits and shutdown/escalation rules. Intermittent or low-pressure supply permits contamination entry through leaks.

3 × 5 = 15, high Pressure logging, leakage repair, safe restart/flushing and water-quality verification. Do not reduce pressure below a validated safe operating range. Flooding or power interruption disables sewage conveyance or inlet pumping. 3 × 5 = 15, high Survey electrical elevations; test safe backup arrangements, alarms, maintenance access and overflow response. Pond overloading, accumulated sludge or short-circuiting worsens effluent quality. 3 × 4 = 12, high Measure flow and loads; inspect hydraulics; survey sludge depth; check actual capacity and discharge requirements before expansion. Our workshop scale is 1–5 for likelihood and consequence; scores 1–4 are low, 5–9 medium, 10–16 high and 17– 25 very high. These are illustrative team judgments, not official CREAT outputs, observed probabilities or financial loss estimates.

Water-safety worksheet to retain with the project We record the hazard, hazardous event, affected users, existing control, control limit, monitoring frequency, responsible role, corrective response and verification record. Utility staff must set actual operating limits from the approved RPAM, treatment design and current requirements. Example entry: “Low source flow during a dry period reduces available supply. We monitor source flow daily during an alert, coordinate distribution and communicate service changes. The operations manager triggers the approved drought response when the locally validated threshold is reached. We record supply hours, pressure, residual disinfectant and complaints, with special attention to health facilities and vulnerable households.” We do not invent a universal chlorine, turbidity, flood-elevation or pressure limit. Those are engineering and public-health control values that require the utility’s system data and applicable standards. Evidence-based worked example | 10

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 2 | Choose actions with reasons After Stage 1, we open View results and continue to action identification. We check that the assessment name is Bandung. In our form review, an earlier assessment’s actions remained visible while the new assessment was incomplete. We do not reuse another case’s action totals or plan. [16] Action Our choice and reason Reduce water loss Select, then narrow the scope to three demonstration DMAs. Published NRW is 39.42% [1]. Confirm physical versus apparent losses and service pressure before estimating benefits. Existing northern-area NRW contract Coordinate before selecting sites. The utility describes a long-term Adaro performance-based contract with a target of 17% NRW from a 2020 northern- area baseline of 45.79% [13]. Do not duplicate contract areas, funding or credited savings. Verify pump performance Select diagnostics for relevant water and wastewater pumps. We lack measured head, flow and input power.

Testing is justified; immediate replacement is not yet justified. Bojongsoang reliability and climate risk Add a custom action. Metering, pond condition, power resilience and flood exposure need verification before expansion or methane investment. Climate-resilient RPAM update Add a custom action. Link drought, wet-weather quality and distribution continuity to the existing plan. 400 additional sewer connections Add as a conditional phase. Proceed only after capacity, effluent performance, network levels, affordability and permissions are verified. Solar PV Defer procurement. Confirm load profiles, site/roof conditions, ownership, grid arrangements and lifecycle cost. A generic percentage saving is not a site design. Aeration optimization Do not select an activated-sludge aeration action for Bojongsoang’s pond train. Inlet pumping and pond performance are the relevant starting points. Biogas capture / covered ponds Select feasibility investigation only within the custom action.

No construction or methane-reduction claim before gas yield, hydraulics, structural design and safety are assessed. Route untreated sewage to treatment Do not infer a real bypass problem or its absence from our assumed zero. Add this action only when measured overflow/bypass evidence and spare treatment capacity support it. Action identifiers and automatic suggestions can change. We select by action title and location, review default savings assumptions, and use Save selected actions. For custom actions, ChatWater states that benefits are not calculated or scientifically reviewed. [16] Evidence-based worked example | 11

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 2 | Copy-ready custom actions Use “+ Add your own action.” Use each heading after “Action B1/B2/B3:” as the Title, then enter the four fields below. The entries fit the displayed character limits. [16] Action B1: Bojongsoang reliability and climate-risk assessment Field Paste this entry What will be done We will verify inlet/outlet meters and pump energy, sample BOD and total nitrogen, survey pond sludge and hydraulic condition, map flood exposure and test emergency power arrangements. We will prepare a prioritized rehabilitation design and a separate methane- capture feasibility decision. Problem addressed Historical flow records do not close the water balance. Current loads, energy, bypasses and pond performance require verification before expansion or emissions-reduction claims. Location Wastewater treatment › Wastewater treatment 1 Notes We model the actual anaerobic–facultative–maturation pond train.

We do not assume activated sludge, zero fugitive methane or safe agricultural reuse. Coordinate with Kabupaten Bandung and relevant river and environmental authorities. Methane works are outside the initial construction budget. Action B2: Climate-resilient RPAM and service-continuity update Field Paste this entry What will be done We will update the existing RPAM with dry-season source-yield and wet-weather water- quality risks, pressure and continuity monitoring, emergency communication, priority-user support and staff drills. We will maintain a linked wastewater flood and power-loss response procedure. Problem addressed Recent source-flow disruption and local flood exposure create plausible service risks. Asset-specific future climate and consequence data are incomplete. Location Whole assessment Notes Use local observations and BMKG projections. The 20% yield reduction and 6-hour outage are stress tests, not forecasts.

Utility staff will approve operating triggers and validate responsibilities. Action B3: Conditional pilot of 400 sewer connections Field Paste this entry What will be done We will survey an eligible sewered catchment and develop 400 proposed connections. Construction proceeds only after treatment-capacity and effluent checks, network design, consent, affordability support and funding approval. Problem addressed Some households may remain unconnected even where a feasible sewer connection exists. The eligible sites and actual beneficiaries are not yet confirmed. Location Wastewater collection › Wastewater collection 1 Notes We allow IDR 3.2 billion using the historical 2024 grant amount per connection as a rough reference, not a current quotation. If capacity or safeguard checks fail, defer this phase and rescope the budget; do not force new inflow into an overloaded system. Evidence-based worked example | 12

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 3 | Project summary and fields 1–4 Project summary We propose a 104-week Tirtawening water-loss and wastewater-reliability pilot. We will establish a measured baseline, work in three water DMAs outside or formally coordinated with the existing northern-area NRW contract, assess and improve selected sewer/WWTP reliability controls, update the RPAM for climate risks, and conditionally connect 400 households. The illustrative investment envelope is IDR 10 billion. Sites, engineering quantities, financing and all benefit estimates remain subject to verification. 1. Define the project Our objective is to improve dry-season water-service reliability and wet-weather wastewater-service continuity while reducing avoidable losses and energy use. Our demonstration scope is three DMAs with approximately 3,000 water connections, selected pump and control assets, Bojongsoang diagnostics and limited rehabilitation, and up to 400 new sewer connections.

All scope quantities are assumptions. We exclude a new treatment plant, complete pond reconstruction and methane-capture construction from this initial budget. 2. Establish the baseline We retain the published 2023 water context: 39.42% NRW, 18 supply hours/day and 169,373 customers. These company indicators are not the measured baseline for the chosen pilot zones. We collect at least eight weeks of initial DMA flow, pressure, billing and pump data, supported by available 12-month records. We reconcile Bojongsoang inflow/outflow, bypasses, BOD, nitrogen, electricity and sludge records. The 2019 wastewater proxy and assumed electricity inputs are replaced before claiming project benefits. We document wet/dry-season differences and data quality. If adequate historical records are unavailable, we extend baseline monitoring before fixing benefits or construction scope. 3.

Identify project activities We confirm the contract and asset boundary; calibrate meters; undertake leak detection, repairs and appropriate pressure management; verify pump duty and efficiency; inspect ponds and sludge; complete flood and power-risk screening; update operating and emergency procedures; prepare designs and procurement; execute justified limited works; and monitor performance. New sewer connections are a conditional work package. Methane capture remains a feasibility question, not a guaranteed mitigation activity. 4. Assign responsibilities We propose Tirtawening’s designated project manager as accountable lead, supported by water-distribution, wastewater-operations, engineering, laboratory, finance and procurement functions. A specialist consultant supports hydraulic, climate, environmental and economic analysis. Kota Bandung supports public coordination and financing discussions;

Kabupaten Bandung and relevant authorities are consulted for works affecting the plant location and receiving waters. We confirm actual mandates, named staff, land rights and approvals before implementation. No organization has committed through this example. Evidence-based worked example | 13

CHATWATER RESILIENCE | TIRTAWENING BANDUNG Stage 3 | Fields 5–8 5. Develop the implementation schedule We plan 104 weeks from confirmed funding and authorization. Weeks 1–8 establish data and responsibilities; weeks 9–16 complete feasibility and design; weeks 17–24 finalize approvals and financing; weeks 25–36 cover procurement; weeks 37–52 cover works and commissioning; and weeks 53–104 verify performance across a full annual cycle. Monitoring begins during baseline development. Procurement and works remain gated by the approved design, environmental requirements and funding. We do not assign a calendar start date before these conditions are met. 6. Define technical and operational requirements We require calibrated bulk and customer meters, timestamped flow/pressure and electricity data, pump duty- point measurements, verified network maps, laboratory quality assurance, pond/sludge surveys and safe access.

Design must preserve drinking-water quality and minimum operating pressure, maintain sewage conveyance during construction and demonstrate treatment capacity before new connections. We include spare parts, staff training, maintenance responsibilities, emergency power arrangements where justified, cybersecurity/access controls for telemetry, and a funded operating budget. Equipment quantities and specifications follow the survey, not this example. 7. Assess implementation risks Our main risks are overlap with the existing NRW contract; inaccurate meters; mistaken estimates of real leakage; dry-season interruption; flood exposure or power loss; pond overloading; construction disruption; land or access constraints; unaffordable household connections; procurement delay; and unfunded maintenance.

We manage these through a contract-boundary review, calibrated baseline, staged works, safe service continuity procedures, early community engagement, affordability assessment and capacity/effluent decision gates. We record residual risk and an accountable owner before procurement. 8. Establish monitoring and evaluation We measure DMA input, billed and unbilled authorized use separately, pressure, supply hours, complaints and repair performance. We compare pump electricity at equivalent hydraulic duty and service output. For wastewater we track metered inflow/outflow, bypass events, BOD and nitrogen loads, effluent results, pond condition and functional new connections. We verify training and emergency exercises. We report baseline, target, result, source, uncertainty and responsible role, with separate water and wastewater beneficiary counts and checks for overlap. We do not claim emissions savings until the baseline, factors and post-project data are accepted.

Review before saving We use Review details, replace generic AI text with these case-specific entries, and resolve or document each missing-data item. A saved draft is not evidence of feasibility, utility approval or funding eligibility. We save the project plan only under the Bandung assessment. [16] Evidence-based worked example | 14
